summary: A proposal by Jon Postel that willing hosts run an Echo process for debugging and measurement. It listens for a connection, completes the Initial Connection Protocol, and sends back whatever data arrives, bit for bit. The connection ends when it is closed. BBN-TENEX already offered such a process.

plainLanguage.summary: Like shouting in a canyon and hearing your own voice come back. A computer repeats back everything you send, which helps check if the connection works.

how does the echo process work
subtitle: Hosts are invited to run a process that sends received data straight back, for debugging and measurement.

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a simple service to help with debugging and measurement of the network.
tldr.mechanism: A willing Host runs a Echo process that waits for a connection, performs the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP), then echoes back all data it receives.
tldr.outcome: The proposal is voluntary: it applies to those hosts which are willing to implement it.

sections.title: The Echo Process Proposal
sections.content: Jon Postel suggests that, for debugging and measurement purposes, those hosts which are willing implement a Echo process. Participation is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers are asked to offer a simple test service, if they want to.

sections.title: How the Echo Process Works
sections.content:
The process listens for a request for connection and executes the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) as specified in NIC 7104, the "Current Network Protocols" notebook. After ICP completes, it waits for data from the network.

When data arrives it is echoed at once and the buffer space is re-allocated. Echoed means the data is sent back over the network, bit for bit, with no modification by the echo process. The process ends when the network connections are closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer waits for someone to knock, says hello the standard way, then sends back exactly what it gets.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: The RFC notes that BBN-TENEX has had such an echo process available for use for a long time. It is a short suggestion from Jon Postel at UCLA and sets no other requirements: any Host that is willing may implement the process, and no Host is required to.
sections.plainLanguage: It is just a friendly suggestion, not a rule.
